plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 3: Organic Compounds: Alkanes and Their Stereochemistry
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a grouped vertical bar chart on a pale blue plotting field comparing two thermal properties of the straight-chain alkanes. The horizontal axis, labeled Number of carbons, carries fourteen categories numbered 1 through 14. The vertical axis, labeled Temperature (degrees C), runs from -200 at the bottom to 300 at the top with labeled gridlines every 100 degrees, and the bars grow upward or downward from the zero gridline. A legend in the upper left assigns blue to Melting point and magenta to Boiling point, and each carbon number carries one bar of each color, blue on the left and magenta on the right. Both series climb steadily from left to right. The blue melting-point bars begin near -180 at one carbon and stay below zero until the last two categories, where they finally reach and just cross the zero line. The magenta boiling-point bars start near -165, rise past zero at four carbons, and continue to roughly 250 at fourteen carbons. In every pair the magenta bar stands taller than the blue one, and the vertical gap between the two widens toward the right of the chart. The plot backs the observation that both transition temperatures increase with molecular size, since the dispersion forces holding molecules together grow as the chain lengthens.

interactionPlan.concept: As straight-chain alkanes get longer, both melting points and boiling points generally rise because larger molecules experience stronger dispersion forces, with boiling points remaining higher than melting points.

demo_steps.title: Start with methane
demo_steps.narration: At one carbon, both bars are far below 0 °C, showing that methane has very low melting and boiling points. The boiling point is still higher than the melting point.

demo_steps.title: Watch boiling points cross 0 °C first
demo_steps.narration: Around four to five carbons, the magenta boiling-point bars reach and pass the zero line while the blue melting-point bars remain far below it. This shows that alkanes become harder to boil before they become solids at room-like temperatures.

demo_steps.title: Compare the melting-point trend
demo_steps.narration: Emphasizing the blue bars makes the melting trend easier to follow: melting points also rise overall, but they stay below 0 °C until the longest chains shown.

demo_steps.title: Longer chains have stronger attractions
demo_steps.narration: By fourteen carbons, both thermal properties are much higher than they were for the smallest alkanes. The growing bars summarize the effect of increasing molecular size and stronger dispersion forces.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Longer alkane chains have stronger intermolecular attractions, so both melting and boiling points rise, but boiling points remain higher and cross 0 °C much earlier.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the chart as a grouped vertical bar chart on a pale blue background. Use blue for melting point bars and magenta for boiling point bars, with blue bars on the left and magenta bars on the right in each carbon-number group. The y-axis should span -200 to 300 °C with clear horizontal gridlines and a visible zero line. Both series rise from left to right; melting points begin around -180 °C and remain negative until the last two carbon counts, while boiling points begin around -165 °C, cross 0 °C near four carbons, and reach about 250 °C by fourteen carbons. Keep the legend in the upper left. The selected carbon count should visibly outline or glow both bars in that group and show compact value labels near the bar ends; the emphasis toggle should brighten the chosen series and fade the other without hiding it.

authoredContext:
Alkanes show regular increases in both boiling point and melting point as molecular weight increases (the figure), an effect due to the presence of weak dispersion forces between molecules (another section). Only when sufficient energy is applied to overcome these forces does the solid melt or liquid boil. As you might expect, dispersion forces increase as molecular size increases, accounting for the higher melting and boiling points of larger alkanes.

A plot of melting and boiling points versus number of carbon atoms for the C1–C14 straight-chain alkanes. There is a regular increase with molecular size.

A double bar graph of temperature versus the number of carbon atoms that plots bars for melting and boiling points with an increasing trend.

Another effect seen in alkanes is that increased branching lowers an alkane’s boiling point. Thus, pentane has no branches and boils at 36.1 °C, isopentane (2-methylbutane) has one branch and boils at 27.85 °C, and neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane) has two branches and boils at 9.5 °C. Similarly, octane boils at 125.7 °C, whereas isooctane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) boils at 99.3 °C. Branched-chain alkanes are lower-boiling because they are more nearly spherical than straight-chain alkanes, have smaller surface areas, and consequently have smaller dispersion forces.

discrepancies: The default view dims the melting-point series with transparency and highlights carbon 1 with a dashed rectangle and numeric callout labels, whereas the source shows all bars uniformly opaque with no selected-carbon annotation.
The legend is laid out horizontally above the plot area on a white background, while the source legend is stacked vertically inside the light-blue chart region at the upper left.

The generated chart includes extra instructional UI, step narration, emphasis controls, hover/click behavior, and value labels that are not present in the static source and make the default view less like a drop-in replacement.
The blue melting bars appear much paler than the source because of the emphasis setting, changing the visual weight of one of the two primary data series.
The plot area is compressed horizontally by the right-side control panel, so the overall composition differs noticeably from the wide source chart.
evaluation.notes: The underlying grouped bar chart, axes, data trends, and labels are mostly correct, but the default view is visually altered by dimming, selection callouts, a misplaced legend, and extra instructional overlays.
action_items: Make the default state match the source: all melting and boiling bars should be fully opaque with no dashed selection box or value callout labels visible initially.
Move the legend into the upper-left of the light-blue plot area and stack the two entries vertically to match the reference.
Preserve the original wide chart composition by minimizing or auto-docking the UI so the plotted figure is not visually compressed.
Use the source-like solid blue and magenta colors consistently unless the user actively enables an emphasis mode.

feedback.rationale: The chart concept and data are correct, but the default rendering has implementation-level fidelity issues—extra UI/callouts, dimmed colors, legend placement, and compressed layout—that the generator can fix.
